title: Mental Accounting
description: We treat money differently depending on where it came from, where it’s kept, or what we intend to use it for—even though all money is the same.
shortDescription: We treat money differently depending on where it came from, where it’s kept, or what we intend to use it for—even though all money is the same.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: We treat money differently depending on where it came from, where it’s kept, or what we intend to use it for—even though all money is the same.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: You get a tax refund of $2,000 and splurge on a luxury item, whereas you’d never do that with $2,000 from your regular savings.
You keep a vacation fund earning 0.5% interest while carrying a credit card balance at 20% interest, because the money is “for” the vacation.
You drive 20 minutes to save $10 on a $50 purchase, but not on a $500 purchase, though the savings are identical.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Assigning windfall money (gifts, bonuses) a “fun” label and spending it freely.
Separating budgets rigidly even when it makes no financial sense.
Treating credit card purchases as less “real” than cash.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “I’m using my bonus money for that.”
“It’s in my savings, so I can’t touch it.” (while paying interest elsewhere)
“It was a gift, so I can treat myself.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You have savings accounts while simultaneously having high‑interest debt.
You spend more with a credit card than you would with cash.
You view money from certain sources as “free” even though it’s part of your total wealth.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Richard Thaler’s concept shows that people categorize funds into non‑fungible mental accounts. This helps with self‑control but creates irrational outcomes when accounts interfere with optimal allocation.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Consolidate your view of money: all dollars are equal.
Pay off high‑interest debt first before building low‑interest savings.
When spending, ask: “Would I buy this if it came from my main bank account, with cash?”

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Thinking mental accounting is just a budgeting tool. It becomes harmful when it prevents paying debt or maximizing returns.
Labeling all windfall money as “extra” rather than part of your net worth.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A couple has a $5,000 holiday fund in a low‑interest account while carrying $5,000 in credit card debt at 18%. They refuse to use the holiday money to pay the debt because it’s “for the trip.” Over a year, they lose hundreds in interest—far more than any experience the trip could provide.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Money doesn’t know its label. A dollar from a bonus spends exactly like a dollar from salary. Treat them as identical soldiers in the same army.
